I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and, through you, the members of the house for their indulgence. I shall not trespass too long upon the time of the house. It is strange that an hon. member should strongly recommend to the minister and to the deputy minister a group of men, the members of which he was not disposed to name apart from Major Hahn. As it turned out, in the first instance one member was a brother, and later on two brothers were in the combination. In the old days when I used to listen to political discussions in Ontario, we called that nepotism. I do not know what it is called to-day, but it is nothing but patronage being distributed to those who are related to one who happens to be a member of this house. I do not like it. I think it is objectionable. Of course the contract was not signed just at that time, but the negotiations continued.
I have outlined what took place on October 9 and October 19. On October 26, only seven days afterwards, we find the hon. member for Trinity, Major Hahn and Mr. Gordon Plaxton, a brother of the member, on the boat for England. They were following up things very closely. They did not give an opportunity to the minister or the department to inquire whether tenders could be received from other reputable concerns in the Dominion of Canada. These men reached England in the course of a few days and they endeavoured to
The Address-Mr. Anderson

interview members of the War Office with respect to a contract which they hoped to get, and which they since obtained. They kicked their heels around London for about ten days and were unable to obtain an interview. I suppose they took in the sights of Piccadilly, Hyde Park, Pall Mall, and probably a few other places. They became impatient after a while, and a telephone message was sent through to the minister asking for some assistance. That was worked through the Department of External Affairs, and that is how the Prime Minister becomes involved. He lent himself, consciously or unconsciously, to what was going on in the defence department. A letter was written and sent to the High Commissioner in London, the Hon. Mr. Massey. Through him it was handed on in the proper way to the War Office. In that letter Major Hahn was regarded as a representative of this government. I say that the Prime Minister as head of the Department of External Affairs should have been more careful. If he did not know of this; if the responsibility rested solely on Doctor Skelton, then I am sorry that Doctor Skelton, for whom I have the highest regard, has lent himself to this sort of thing.
Why was Major Hahn considered as the representative of this government in connection with contracts for munitions for Great Britain and Canada? This is monstrous. What about our industries in Canada? We hear a great deal of talk about unemployment and relief, but what efforts did they make to get something beneficial out of the money to be spent by the defence department for the manufacture of munitions? What did they do? They put this in the hands of Major Hahn and his associates, who were, unfortunately for the hon. member for Trinity, brothers of a member of this house.
Let me say a word about Major Hahn. He was a good Canadian and, while I am not sure, I believe he is a graduate of Toronto * university. He went overseas, gave good service, and rose in rank. He came back to Canada with imperial rank. He was wounded; he served his country nobly and he is entitled to every credit in that regard. As a man I do not think anything can be said against him to-day, and certainly nothing could be said about him at that time. Upon his return he decided to study law. The law society of Ontario passed a regulation to permit men returning from the front who possessed the necessary qualifications and were desirous of studying law to complete their course in two years. They were to take the same number of lectures and examinations, but the lectures were to be almost continuous.

The usual intervals between lectures were to be eliminated. Major Hahn took that course and became a lawyer. My son was one of those who took advantage of that regulation, and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Factor) was another who took that course. Up to that point these men were all on a par.
Major Hahn became a lawyer, but he decided he would not continue in the practice of law. Industry had a claim on him. We will assume that the war closed in 1919 because many of the important officers did not get back until that year. In 1923, after he had been admitted to practice in Ontario, Major Hahn became interested in the establishment of a concern known as the De Forest Radio Corporation, which carried on business in the constituency represented by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). That company carried on for seven years, and it was represented to the minister and to the War Office as being a successful business financially.
Seven years is not long in the existence or life of an industry. It was a large industry, but when the adverse winds of the depression struck it in 1930 it began losing money. It was under the administration and management of Major Hahn, and it lost money in 1931, 1932 and 1933. The reason was, he said, that competition was so great that he found it necessary to try to sell the business to one of his competitors, which was done. That was the Rogers Majestic, in Toronto, the operators of CFRB. It bought out the De Forest concern, and the major then dropped out of business. That was in 1934. Now what about that business? It went into the hands of a receiver immediately. The claims against the concern amounted to only $140,000, which was not a large amount for a financially successful concern in seven years, and yet when they came to distribute the assets, what was the result? The creditors got the munificent return of twenty cents on the dollar. Nevertheless that is the company which is represented to the minister, to the Department of National Defence and to the War Office in London, as being a successful one. Although it had not been running since 1936, it was represented to the War Office as immediately capable of turning out war material.
I do not want to trespass further, Mr. Speaker, on the indulgence that the house has been good enough to extend to me, but I should like in conclusion to say that the government of Canada should repudiate that contract. If it goes any further, the imperial authorities will feel that Canadians are not worthy of trust in matters so important as the manufacture and purchase of munitions.

The Address-Mr. Clarke (Rosedale)
I am not saying anything against the minister. He is one for whom I have had the greatest respect, but I do say that as a minister of the crown he has not exercised that caution, care, and regard for the welfare of Canada which he should have, and which the responsibility of his office demanded of him. I consider that the work of his deputy was positively reprehensible. I shall not apply that term to the minister. I shall give him some credit for having depended on his experts, as he said himself. But how far has he depended on his experts? It has been shown that he did not depend on them at all; that he did not know with whom he was dealing; that he did not ask tenders, as suggested by the interdepartmental committee, from such concerns as the Steel Company of Canada, the National Steel Car Company, the Dominion Bridge Company and other big companies in this dominion that are capable of carrying on this work, companies that have been in existence for generations and are to-day in a strong financial position and able to carry out government contracts with precision and accuracy, companies in which one can have absolute confidence. I thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, may I first refer briefly to the wonderful speeches that were made by the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Undoubtedly they were the best I have ever heard on such an occasion, more particularly that of the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier), who gave his address in both English and French and with a fluency that I thought could not be surpassed. But a few nights ago I listened to the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon) also delivering an address to the house in English and French, and to my amazement his effort equalled, if not excelled, that of the hon. member for Stormont in its fluency in both languages.
I should also like to compliment the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the good judgment he showed in the selection of his two new cabinet ministers a few days ago. I believe these appointments are very
popular indeed, particularly that of the new Postmaster General, the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. McLarty). I have known him for a long time. I know his genial nature, and how pleasant it is to be in his company. I know how able he has shown himself in getting things done; and in his appointement to the office of Postmaster General the Prime Minister made a wonderful selection.
Turning now to the speech from the throne, after listening to so many able speeches since parliament convened on January 12 last, I think there is little more to be said, but I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without expressing the gratification and the happiness that my constituents in Rosedale riding, Toronto, feel at the forthcoming visit of Their Majesties the King and Queen. Toronto is, I believe, one of the most beautiful cities in the whole world. In population it is the second largest city in this dominion. I have visited many cities in Canada, the United States, Europe, Asia and Africa, and I have always felt on my return to Toronto that not a city I had visited could compare with it at all. I have spoken of the happiness my constituents feel at having their majesties visit the city of Toronto for a short time this spring. But there is always the bitter to be taken with the sweet. Loyal subjects of the king and queen residing in Toronto are looking for an opportunity to greet their majesties, and what do we find? We find that this great city is imposed upon by being granted only the short period of eight hours for their majesties' visit. I do not know where the blame should be placed, or whether it is just another Liberal government error and the public must suffer for it.
I should like to allude briefly to a matter arising from the news received in Ottawa on Monday morning of the resignation by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett of his seat in the House of Commons. For many years he occupied a seat in this house as private member, as cabinet minister, as Prime Minister, and, for the last three years, as leader of the king's loyal opposition, the position he resigned last year. I shall not try to eulogize the many merits of so fine a gentleman and statesman, but I cannot let this opportunity go by without acknowledging his sterling qualities. I have often heard it said that a man is not appreciated until he is dead; but so far as the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett is concerned, he is very much appreciated while alive, and I believe that his name will go down in history as an outstanding statesman and gentleman and a great Canadian Prime Minister.
536	COMMONS
The Address-Air. Clarke (Rosedale)
May I say a few words also with reference to the present leader of the king's loyal opposition in the house (Mr. Manion). I have been in this chamber during the sessions of this eighteenth parliament. During that time I have endeavoured to do my best, and I believe the same is time of every other Conservative member. Our numbers are not very great, and each of us has had to put his shoulder to the wheel; but may I say that since the present leader of the opposition, with his charming disposition, his wonderful personality, his gifts of magnetism and leadership, his power to engage the cooperation of all members of his party, has held his present position, I have never seen such enthusiasm as exists to-day among all our members.
We have seen terrible happenings in Toronto during the past week. Nothing of the kind has occurred before in that city. It is a direct reflection on the inactivity of the present government in connection with unemployment, especially among the youth of our country. I refer to the arrest of a number of young unemployed single men. A few weeks ago, on the orders of the day, I spoke on their behalf to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), and what has happened since makes me wonder where we are going under the administration of this do-nothing government, which leaves our youth to suffer under the appalling burden of unemployment. There is one period in a man's life which either makes or breaks him- the period between seventeen and twenty-one. During that time a young man is moulding his future, and if he is allowed to go about in idleness there is a great possibility that he may do something which will injure him for the rest of his life. May I again urge that the government take immediate action to eliminate, as far as possible, this trouble and not spoil the lives of thousands of fine young Canadians who, if they are given a chance, provided with some useful employment, and not allowed through idleness to fall by the wayside, may be occupying to-morrow the seats which we hold to-jay.
I desire to make a brief reference to the recent trade treaty. To my mind, when the government enters upon treaty making with the United States it is going into pretty capable company, engaging with pretty clever people, people who generally make treaties for the United States and do not worry about the interests of any country other than their own. I do not intend to labour this matter, but I am concerned when I see the quotas which are being put upon exports of our goods to the United States. Imports to Canada from the United States are mostly manufactured

lines, and all the restraint that appears to have been placed by way of quota or any other deterrent upon their goods is the dumping clause. That seems to be the only thing we have done to hinder manufactured goods from being brought into Canada from the United States and taking away the employment of our workers in various lines of industrial production. Last fall, when I made several hundred calls in my riding, I discovered that in the industrial sections more men would be laid off because of this new trade treaty and the removal of the three per cent excise tax.
May I suggest to the government that as soon as possible they take action to abolish this burdensome sales tax of eight per cent which is a direct charge on all the citizens of this dominion. I have been waiting to hear that some legislation in regard to this matter will be introduced in the near future. It is very likely there will be an election before long and the government have made some reductions in the sales tax, but I think they should go further and assist the overburdened taxpayer by removing the tax altogether. In this connection I might quote from a letter, dated January 30, 1939, which I have received from the sales tax repeal association of Bay street, Toronto. It is a long letter and I shall read only a part of it. In reference to the eight per cent sales tax it says:
Not content with charging interest on overdue sales tax, the delinquent is liable for double the tax due, a fine in addition, and imprisonment, and no judge is allowed any discretion in the matter.
Can you imagine any more outrageous treatment of small dealers and struggling concerns than such penalties? These men are not crooks but good citizens, yet they are really treated as worse than criminals.
I shall not go any further in that connection. There is one thing I would mention, however, with regard to the relief problem. This has been a great problem to every municipality throughout the country. Organizations have been set up in every town and city to urge upon the government that they take over all, or at least a part of the relief burden, but so far only a small concession has been made, and most of the burden remains on the municipalities. If the government would remove this tax upon the municipalities, this would solve the housing problem and give employment to thousands of workers, and in a very short time we would return to prosperity. I do not think there is any doubt about that. Both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) have endeavoured to put many schemes into effect, but they have been only partly successful. I suggest that from the standpoint

The Address-Mr. Cleaver
of the private citizen and the businessman, it would be a sound principle to remove the heavy relief tax on properties and buildings. If that were done, building work would be proceeded with and there would be no question of unemployment.
One matter I cannot allow to pass without some comment is the radio tax. I protested last year against the increase in the fee from $2 to $2.50 per set, and where a man has more than one set he has to pay more. I was successful in having the minister agree that where an indigent person on relief had a radio it should not be necessary for that person to buy a licence in order to use his radio. That was only proper and I was pleased that the minister granted the request.
Another subject which I brought up was the freedom with which inspectors could enter private houses. On that point I received support from many fion. members. After all, no matter how small it is, a private house is a man's castle and he should not be bothered by having people running in and out of his home without proper authority. On that occasion I suggested to the minister that there should be an order from a supreme court judge, because I thought that would have a deterrent effect on inspectors. In this respect the minister did not fulfil his promise. When he brought in his bill I was sorry to see that he had omitted that part of it. I shall not go any further now on the radio question; I shall discuss that later when the estimates are under consideration.
I have tried to be as brief as possible. In my opinion the forty minute rule was adopted for speakers who have some special subject to explain-cabinet ministers and the like-and I am sure that the session could be considerably shortened if hon. members would be brief and not exceed the forty minutes. If hon. members would curtail their remarks as far as they reasonably could, there would be a saving of many thousands of dollars to the Canadian taxpayer.

The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Clarke) and other members representing urban ridings in Ontario have expressed great concern over the disastrous results to industry from the 1935 United States-Canada trade agreement, and their apprehension of the impending results, equally disastrous, that will flow from the three-way agreement that has recently been consummated. I have some figures which will possibly put their minds at rest on that score. If they turn up the record of industrial building during the period of the Bennett administration and then look at the
record of what has happened since in such building, I think hon. gentlemen who sit across from me will have their minds put at rest in regard to the effect of the trade agreement on industry. During the ten year period ending in 1930 Ontario industries expended an annual average of a little more than $15,000,000 on capital outlays for factories, warehouses and the like. Then during the five year period of the Bennett administration what do we find? We find that in 1931 industry was so confident upon the coming into power of the Bennett administration that it cut its expenditures on factory buildings in half. In that year industry expended $6,836,000 on capital outlay. In 1932 we reached an all-time low, less than $2,000,000, the figure for that year being $1,871,000. In 1933 there was some recovery; $4,700,000 was expended. In 1934 we slipped again, down to $4,306,000. In 1935 we slipped further, to $3,645,000. For the five years the total spent in Ontario on factory and industrial construction was $21,358,000, or a yearly average of $4,271,600.
After the Liberal administration came into office in October, 1935, and negotiated the United States trade pact of 1935 "which came into force on January 1, 1936, what happened? We all know that capitalists spend money in expanding their factories only when their business is expanding and when they have confidence in the future. In 1937 Ontario industries were so impoverished by the trade agreement and their owners so alarmed that in that year they actually increased their factory construction expenditures to over four times the 1931-35 average, or an amount greater than was spent in any year during the Bennett administration. In 1937 Ontario industrialists spent $17,933,000 in factory construction work. We not only equalled the average annual construction for the ten-year period from 1921 to 1930. but exceeded that average by over $2,000,000. This voluntary response by Ontario industry, in my opinion, answers once and for all the Tory charge that the United States trade agreement was harmful to industry in Canada. I suggest that it also accounts for the fact that the new Great Britain-United States-Canada trade agreement has met with practically no criticism by industry. But one thing left unexplained is the loud and continuous complaint by Conservative members with respect to the treaty. The reason for this I quite confidently leave to the good judgment of the electors.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
